We present DART, a highly efficient, robust, and simple policy iteration algorithm for maximizing the overall mean of individual reward functions. DART iteratively samples and incorporates a set of random reward function combinations, and through theoretical analysis, we demonstrate its ability to achieve a $O(1/\varepsilon)$ iteration complexity and $O(\log(1/\varepsilon))$ sample complexity for optimizing $L_{\infty}$-smooth reward functions to within $\varepsilon$ of optimal. DART's sample-based approach allows it to adapt to noisy samples and can be applied to non-smooth reward functions by adding a smooth penalty, resulting in a $O(1/\varepsilon)$ iteration complexity and $O(\varepsilon^{-4} \log(1/\varepsilon))$ sample complexity. DART's effectiveness is further validated through empirical comparisons with existing methods, and its ability to handle noisy samples is also illustrated through experimental results. Moreover, DART's theoretical sample complexity for optimizing non-smooth reward functions is also supported by our experiments. Additionally, DART's performance is also compared with DART-based methods that utilize a smooth penalty, and our results show that DART-based methods can achieve better results with less noisy samples. Mobile Augmented Reality applications are becoming increasingly prominent due to the rapid advancement of mobile devices' hardware capabilities. However, these applications often necessitate significant computational resources and necessitate for mobile devices to access cloud servers for offloading tasks, which may not always be feasible, particularly in rapidly changing environments where user movement can cause disruptions in task offloading. To address this limitation, we introduce Mobile-Net-Util, a framework that optimizes cloud-server utilization by dividing and scheduling essential tasks in line with changing network conditions. We also propose a deep reinforcement learning-based offloading strategy that considers network fluctuations and demonstrate its effectiveness through comprehensive simulations, showing that our approach minimizes task completion time and enhances overall system performance. The results highlight the superiority of Mobile-Net-Util compared to existing offloading strategies. Furthermore, our experiments reveal that Mobile-Net-Util's service decomposition capability significantly enhances system efficiency, particularly in scenarios with rapid user movement, resulting in significant reductions in task completion time. Additionally, we observe that the framework's service decomposition capability proves beneficial even in slow-changing environments, resulting in moderate performance enhancements. The experiments also show that Mobile-Net-Util's offloading strategy outperforms baseline methods, particularly in environments with rapid user movement, resulting in significant reductions in task completion time and system energy consumption. To facilitate reproducibility, we have publicly released our framework's source code on GitHub at https://github.com/azharali/Mobile-Net-Util. We introduce a novel gravity model, corrected for infrared effects, and develop a corresponding cosmological framework within the metric $f(R)$ theory. The modified model, inspired by Starobinsky's theory, incorporates a term proportional to $(\Box R - \frac{1}{6}R_{\mu\nu}\Box R_{\mu\nu} - \frac{1}{3}\Box^2R)$, and we demonstrate its equivalence to a $f(R)$ gravity model. We apply Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) analysis to the IRG model, utilizing the Planck 2018 data sets, and find that it outperforms the ΛCDM model in several key metrics, including goodness of fit, parameters, and empirical evidence. We introduce a method to objectively assess the performance of such filters by analyzing the correlation between the high and low-resolution components.
The new metric, named $k$-correlation, is simple to calculate and can be used to evaluate a wide range of image filtering techniques.
We apply our approach to several well-known image filtering methods, comparing their outcomes to those of our reference blurring and sharpening algorithms.
Furthermore, we conduct an experiment to investigate how users perceive the differences in image quality when using various filtering techniques that achieve similar $k$-correlation values. 
Our results show that the new metric effectively reflects human perception of image quality. 
The approach can be further extended to other image processing tasks.

Recent breakthroughs in the field of Representation Learning have led to innovative approaches to Generalization, allowing for the development of more effective models that excel in a variety of tasks.  In this study, we investigate the potential of using a new metric, the Representation Manifold Quality Score (RMQM), to assess the generalization abilities of these models.  Specifically, we focus on the Quality of the Representation Space, as opposed to the Space it contains.  Our findings demonstrate that the RMQM can predict a model's performance in downstream tasks and its resistance to adversarial attacks, without needing to access the tasks or attacks during training.  Our results are consistent across various models, datasets, and evaluation metrics, providing a more generalizable and transferable method for assessing representation quality.  Our research further highlights the need for a more comprehensive approach to generalization, one that goes beyond simply minimizing the distance between representations and their corresponding labels.  Ultimately, we believe that the RMQM has the potential to become a valuable tool in the field of Representation Learning, enabling the development of more effective models that generalize well to unseen data. This is particularly relevant for robots equipped with low-resolution or no camera systems, such as those relying on joystick or joystick-free control. Consequently, we developed a teleoperation system that enables participants to feel forces generated by virtual objects manipulated via robotic systems, allowing them to perceive and adapt to the robot's dynamics. A validation study involving 20 participants revealed that our system significantly enhances dexterity in tasks requiring force-based manipulation, considering factors like distance, object size, and participant experience. This achievement paves the way for future applications involving teleoperation of robots via joystick or other input methods. Additionally, we discovered that our system's effectiveness lies in its ability to convey the robot's internal state, including contact information and forces exerted onto the object. This internal state information is crucial for participants to successfully manipulate objects at a distance. A notable finding is that our participants' performance in force-based manipulation tasks was comparable to that of human-human collaboration, which highlights the system's potential for use in training operators for teleoperation of robots under contact-rich scenarios. Lastly, we found that our participants developed a unique representation of the robot's dynamics, distinct from that of a human operator. This representation is crucial for participants to effectively manipulate objects at a distance. Overall, our study demonstrates the system's potential for remote operators to acquire and utilize complex robotic systems, ultimately leading to improved performance in force-based manipulation tasks. We believe that our contribution has significant implications for the development of teleoperation systems, particularly in scenarios involving contact-rich tasks and the manipulation of objects at a distance. A novel method for evaluating dehazed image quality is presented, which uses reduced-reference quality assessment to quantify the perceived quality of dehazed images in terms of naturalness. By applying a spatial pre-processing technique, the original image's local features are extracted and condensed into a reduced-reference format. Dehazed images are then re-mapped onto these features, allowing for reduced-reference evaluation of dehazed image quality. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach effectively measures both the dehazing process and dehazed image quality, outperforming leading reduced-reference and full-reference evaluation methods in terms of correlation with human perception. Furthermore, the proposed method exhibits flexibility in handling various dehazing techniques, which is an uncommon advantage among reduced-reference evaluation methods. In addition, the method's source and target features can be easily modified to accommodate other image processing operations, such as image compression, for task-adaptive evaluation. All related resources, including source code and demo videos, are available online. An accompanying video is also included to demonstrate the method's flexibility in addressing common image compression artifacts. Implementation details can be found in the accompanying FPGM code. Deep learning models have become increasingly influential in the field of computer vision and have been widely adopted in mobile applications. Despite their importance, the security of these models has not been thoroughly explored, particularly in the context of adversarial attacks. This study aims to fill this knowledge gap by conducting a comprehensive analysis of the resilience of mobile deep learning applications to adversarial attacks. We examine a dataset of 1, 964 mobile applications and subject their underlying deep learning models to white-box and black-box attacks. Our results indicate that a significant proportion of these applications are vulnerable to attacks, with white-box attacks affecting up to 71% and black-box attacks affecting up to 39% of them. Furthermore, our study reveals that a small group of model owners possess a substantial amount of influence over their respective app stores' rankings, which could be exploited by malicious actors. We also propose several potential mitigation strategies to enhance the security of these models. Our research contributes to the existing knowledge on adversarial attacks and provides insights that can inform developers, researchers, and mobile app store operators on how to improve the resilience of deep learning models to such attacks. We hope that our findings will raise awareness about the potential risks and motivate the community to take necessary steps to protect these models. Deep survival models have been widely applied in healthcare, particularly in predicting patient survival, for their accuracy and precision. Nevertheless, the complex workings of these models make it challenging to interpret their predictions, ultimately hindering their application in clinical settings. To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach, called reverse survival model (RSM), that enhances the explainability of predictions made by existing deep survival models. RSM operates by generating a patient population with the same survival distribution as the original data and matching it to the patient population in the test set based on time-dependent censoring. Consequently, RSM transforms the complex predictor into a combination of the surrogate dataset, allowing for a more understandable representation of predictions that can be applied in various scenarios, including survival trees and providing actionable insights for clinicians. Our experiments on real-world survival datasets show that RSM not only improves the explainability of predictions but also maintains the accuracy of survival predictions. Additionally, we showcase the practical value of RSM by applying it to a real-world patient population, demonstrating its potential to identify high-risk patients and offer actionable recommendations. This paper explores the estimation of a moving object's orientation in a 3D space using multiple UWB radios and calculates the time delay of signal reflection off nearby surfaces. To account for the interference caused by multiple signal paths, a novel approach is proposed that models the error in orientation estimation due to noisy data and varying signal conditions at each UWB device. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of this method in achieving accurate orientation estimates across different scenarios with multiple UWB radios and varying levels of signal interference. A real-world experiment conducted indoors shows that the proposed technique can estimate the orientation of a vehicle with high accuracy despite signal interference, and its performance is compared to existing orientation estimation methods. To further improve orientation accuracy, a machine learning-based approach is proposed that combines UWB signal data with GPS information to estimate the orientation of a vehicle. This technique is evaluated using a dataset from an indoor test and shows a significant improvement in orientation estimation accuracy when combined with GPS information. As a result, the proposed approach provides a more reliable method for determining vehicle orientation in a 3D space using UWB technology. Moreover, the proposed machine learning-based technique significantly outperforms traditional orientation estimation methods, achieving a mean absolute error of 4.2 degrees, which is approximately a 50% reduction from the baseline method. This research has the potential to be applied in various fields, such as robotics and self-driving cars. A dataset collected during this research is made available to the academic community for further research purposes. To facilitate reproducibility of the results, the UWB data, GPS information, and a Python implementation of the proposed methods are made available online. This research introduces a unified control method for legged robots that integrate walking and manipulation. The approach involves a model predictive control system that combines the dynamics of the robot with the external environment. By using contact force minimization, the control method enables the robot to interact with objects in its surrounding space. Through simulations of a legged robot manipulating a box, the effectiveness of the control method is demonstrated by achieving a high level of precision in path tracing. Specifically, it achieves a 50% increase in the overall network speed across different wireless conditions, with a direct link established between this hybrid approach and the available bandwidth. We introduce an executable monitoring system for multi-level process specifications that encapsulates and bridges different process models, focusing on providing explanations and justifications for violations of each other's constraints during runtime. 
When a system monitored by our tool violates some constraint at runtime, our approach involves identifying the most relevant constraint violation that impacts the compliance issue at hand and providing a joint explanation for both violations. 
This allows us to quantify the severity of each individual violation by evaluating its contribution to the overall compliance issue. 
As a result, our system offers a way to address conflicts between different process specifications during execution by providing a joint explanation for violations and measuring the contribution of each to the compliance issue. 
We demonstrate the practicality of this approach through a case study, and showcase the system's capabilities through a video available at \url{https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V1Lz1V8T4F0}.

Existing secure multi-authority attribute-based encryption (SMABE) schemes are vulnerable to coercion attacks. When users are forced to reveal their secret keys, adversaries can obtain unencrypted messages. To address this issue, we introduce Wink, a SMABE scheme that enables users to conceal the encrypted message content even under coercion. Wink achieves this through innovative design of ciphertexts that include additional components. These components are derived from a pseudorandom function that remains secret even after an adversary accesses the user's secret key. Unlike prior SMABE schemes, Wink does not rely on a single, trusted authority and instead relies on a more practical assumption that users will not reveal their entire secret key. To evaluate Wink's performance, we implemented it on a Raspberry Pi 4B model B and found that it can process user attribute vectors composed of up to 250 bits in just 1.5 seconds while maintaining confidentiality. To further assess its security, we conducted a formal analysis of Wink using a custom abstraction of the underlying pseudorandom function. Our analysis revealed that Wink provides robust security against a wide range of adversarial scenarios, including those that involve coercion attacks. To verify this, we conducted a practical experiment that demonstrated Wink's ability to protect user confidentiality even after an adversary accesses the entire secret key. These results confirm that Wink offers superior security against coercion attacks compared to existing SMABE schemes. Furthermore, ISLET provides clear theoretical assurances regarding convergence, stability, and error bounds. Reducing the density of logical syndromes is a viable strategy for implementing globally decodable codes on a noisy quantum computer, as it allows for the use of global decoding methods that are resistant to faulty gate operations. However, the current state of quantum technology, characterised by limited qubit density and faulty quantum memory, necessitates the development of efficient methods to achieve this reduction, given the substantial output from logical measurements. In this work, we introduce a novel post-processing technique that leverages the graph structure of logical measurements to identify the minimum set of syndrome bits required to accurately determine the logical syndrome. By utilising this technique, we are able to demonstrate that the logical syndrome can be significantly reduced, often by a factor of 10, without compromising the accuracy or speed of decoding. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the post-processing technique can be performed using classical hardware alone, making it a scalable solution for practical quantum computing applications. Additionally, we demonstrate the potential of our method by applying it to the surface code and show that the post-processing technique can be used to significantly reduce the logical syndrome density for a 64-qubit code with over 64,000 input measurements. Our work represents a crucial step towards the practical implementation of quantum error correction on near-term quantum hardware. By utilizing the somewhat homomorphic encryption technique, we enable the server to conduct general computations with encrypted user data, keeping users' locations undisclosed. Additionally, our approach supports a hybrid client-based solution, where client devices conduct calculations locally with partially encrypted server data, minimizing data exchange between clients and servers. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our protocol through a simulation that compares various general computation scenarios with traditional solutions like the Gaussian mixture model and reveal its superior performance in precision and speed. Moreover, our protocol can be integrated with deep learning-based services, as shown through a case study involving indoor localization. Experimental results show that our approach yields comparable performance to state-of-the-art solutions in terms of accuracy, while significantly enhancing user privacy and data protection. Our solution is open-source, even including the employed deep learning models, to promote transparency and reproducibility. In this study, we explore the application of federated learning in settings where data changes over time. Each participant receives new data sequences at distinct time points, and must adapt its learned function accordingly. Participants can share their updated functions with a central server, which aggregates them into a single, combined function. Our goal is to design an online federated learning approach that balances individual data privacy with rapid convergence. Building upon a previous, albeit suboptimal, framework, we develop a novel online federated learning algorithm that achieves a more efficient regret bound in terms of the number of steps taken. Additionally, we apply this method to a more complex scenario involving non-stationary data that evolves according to a controlled Markov process. Our algorithm's convergence to the optimal function is guaranteed and its non-asymptotic regret bounds are derived for both scenarios. Furthermore, we provide theoretical justifications for its performance in the non-stationary setting. Finally, we validate our approach through experiments on a variety of real-world datasets. Our findings show that our proposed method outperforms existing techniques, such as the online federated learning method, in terms of convergence speed. However, we also observe that our method's performance is affected by the number of participants, which may not be desirable in some applications. Therefore, we propose a modified, decentralized variant of our method that achieves similar performance while minimizing the impact of the number of participants. Specifically, backdoor attacks pose a significant threat, as they can be injected into models during training and remain undetected. Existing research has focused on developing backdoor attack detection methods, but they often struggle to account for the nuances of real-world data distribution. In this paper, we present an innovative approach to detecting backdoor attacks, leveraging the fact that such malware can be easily re-injected into a model after a successful attack. By analyzing the distribution of activation scores from multiple network layers, our approach can accurately detect malicious models. In contrast to traditional methods, our approach is effective even in scenarios with limited training data and adversarial data augmentation. Our experiments demonstrate the efficacy of SmartWatcher in detecting backdoor attacks, outperforming state-of-the-art methods in various settings. Moreover, our approach can be adapted to other types of malicious attacks, such as feature attack, and is resistant to common data augmentation techniques. to define the specific rules of the translation grammar.

capture the complex relationships between the different code elements.

mirrors human coding practices in multiple aspects, including the optimal use
of coding practices and the ability to define abstract coding concepts. 
Lastly, we've discovered that the model's performance can be significantly
enhanced by fine-tuning it with real-world examples of code translations. 
This fine-tuning process, known as learning from examples, is a relatively
straightforward and efficient process.

Reinforcement Learning (RL) has proven itself to be a powerful tool in solving complex, sequential decision-making problems, but its effectiveness can be hindered by insufficient access to high-quality training data. To address this challenge, Federated Reinforcement Learning (FRL) emerges as a viable solution by enabling the collaboration of multiple agents, each utilizing their local data to generate improved policies while keeping their information private. By leveraging this collaborative approach, FRL not only enhances RL performance but also guarantees data privacy for each agent. In this study, we conduct an in-depth examination of FRL, commencing with an overview of its key components and the various types of FRL frameworks. We subsequently discuss FRL challenges, drawing on a comprehensive survey of existing literature and the experiences of different FRL frameworks. To shed light on the potential of FRL, we also present several case studies of its applications in finance, robotics, and other domains. Finally, we conclude by highlighting the current shortcomings and future research avenues in the realm of FRL. This work aims to provide a comprehensive overview of FRL, serving as a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners in the field. We hope that this survey will foster further innovation in FRL and inspire new applications in the field. This approach is also compared to alternative representations based on event structures and Petri nets. Specifically, we argue that ctrees offer a more suitable framework for capturing parallelism in higher-order concurrent systems. Initially, both contact and condensed pair fractions increase in tandem, only to plateau and shift in line with the gas's growing density. Ultimately, they both settle at a single value that reflects the ratio of the trap's expansion rate to the particles' mass. Conversely, the two-time correlation function displays a more complex pattern, its long-distance and short-time behavior mirroring that of the contact, but its short-distance behavior mirroring that of the condensed pair fraction. Recent breakthroughs in transformer-based models have led to outstanding performance across a wide array of tasks. However, these achievements have come at a cost due to the high computational requirements and low efficiency of traditional self-attention mechanisms. In an effort to overcome this limitation, a novel approach called DAE-Former has been developed. Based on the Decoupled and Adaptive Encoding (DAE) framework, DAE-Former has been designed to decouple the tasks of decoding and encoding in a sequential process. In a first step, a low-dimensional feature space is created through a process of data encoding. Next, a self-attention module is used to derive the final output. Furthermore, DAE-Former incorporates a dynamic masking strategy to dynamically regulate the scope of self-attention. Through rigorous testing on benchmark datasets, DAE-Former has been proven to deliver exceptional results while minimizing processing costs. In comparison to existing models, DAE-Former has been shown to achieve a 1.2% improvement in accuracy while reducing the number of FLOPs required by nearly 80%. Additionally, DAE-Former has been successfully applied to tasks involving 3D point clouds, speech recognition, and multiple other tasks. In each instance, DAE-Former has been found to deliver results that are at least as good as, if not superior to, the current state-of-the-art methods. In fact, DAE-Former has been found to be the most computationally efficient of all the models tested, making it an ideal choice for real-world applications. Understanding how proteins interact across species is a complex task, particularly when it comes to understanding how viruses adapt to the host immune system. Traditional protein family clustering methods can be too restrictive, focusing only within a single host's proteins and failing to capture the relationships between viral and host proteins. By applying this network method to viral proteins and human immune system proteins, we were able to identify key biological processes disrupted by different SARS-CoV-2 strains and compare them to those of other coronaviruses. Our results, combined with additional insights from protein sequence analysis, provide a more comprehensive understanding of how SARS-CoV-2 has evolved to infect humans. This network approach offers a more nuanced interpretation of protein sequence conservation and divergence, highlighting the importance of considering both global and local protein interactions in the context of protein function. Our method can be applied to a wide range of viral proteins and host systems for a more detailed understanding of protein relationships. To ensure seamless human-robot collaboration, robots must consider the actions they perform, resulting in minimal disruptions to humans. This paper presents a novel learning-based approach called Collaborative Skill Embedding (CSE), which enables mobile robots to develop collision-free and efficient navigation skills in dense human environments without requiring extensive training or reward engineering. Using novel, specially designed training simulations, the proposed method enables robots to learn to adapt their motion planning by considering the proximity of moving humans in real-time. This results in a reduction of collisions and a natural limitation on the speed of interaction, making the navigation more human-centered and comfortable. Through simulation experiments, the effectiveness of CSE is demonstrated, showcasing its ability to produce robust and efficient navigation policies for mobile robots in various human-robot interaction scenarios. Additionally, the proposed method was successfully tested in real-world experiments, resulting in a significant reduction in collisions with moving humans. This work marks the first time a learning-based approach has been used to develop collision-free and efficient navigation skills in mobile robots operating in dense human settings. As a result, the proposed method offers a promising solution for the development of autonomous and natural human-robot collaboration in real-world settings. Recent studies have demonstrated that deep face recognition models are highly susceptible to backdoor attacks, which involve training-time manipulations of models using malicious samples. These studies have shown that these attacks can compromise the models' performance on clean test data, making them vulnerable to targeted threats. To counter this issue, we introduce a novel approach called BA-BAM, which integrates both adversarial training and a clean-backdoor mechanism into face recognition models to enhance their robustness against backdoor attacks. This approach utilizes a novel clean-backdoor trigger that incorporates a clean image feature to create malicious samples. To defend against these attacks, BA-BAM employs a detector module to identify samples generated by the backdoor mechanism and a clean-backdoor module to generate clean samples using the detector's output. Experimental results on three datasets across various attack scenarios have shown that BA-BAM outperforms existing methods in terms of classification accuracy and threat tolerance. Additionally, our approach outperforms existing methods in terms of classification accuracy when the training data is partially corrupted by malicious samples. A common approach to simplifying 3D point clouds is to apply a non-parametric smoothing technique. However, most methods rely on local neighborhood-based or grid filters that struggle to maintain the accuracy and smoothness of the original surface. To address this, we've developed a novel hypergraph-based approach that leverages edge and node properties to preserve the surface topology while achieving a level of simplification. Our hypergraph spectral filter enables the reduction of points while retaining key features, and we can control the level of simplification using a Lasso matrix. We also introduce a loss function that minimizes the difference between the original and simplified geometric structures. To speed up the computation, we've developed a scalable algorithm that optimizes the extraction of the k-th principal eigenbasis. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in preserving the surface topology while achieving a balanced trade-off between simplicity and accuracy. In the field of surgical robotics, accurately estimating needle and trocar poses is essential for successful keyhole procedures. To address this need, we've developed an innovative image-based solution that utilizes a deep learning approach to achieve high-precision pose estimation. By integrating a fully convolutional network and a spatial transformer module, our system can efficiently and accurately localise surgical tools in 2D and 3D space. To enhance generalisability and expand application areas, we've trained our network with data from diverse tools and paths. Furthermore, we've successfully integrated our spatial transformer module, allowing for dynamic tool path adaptation and efficient training. To validate our approach, we've conducted experiments using 1725 images from 30 publicly available sequences. The goal of 3D reconstruction from multiple images is to infer a scene's 3D shape from various views. Recent advancements have leveraged deep learning to learn features from images and reconstruct 3D models without pre-existing knowledge. Despite this progress, a lack of real-world benchmarks hampers the development of learned multi-view 3D reconstruction methods. To address this limitation, a new benchmark called SceneFusion is presented, utilizing high-quality 3D scans of everyday scenes. This dataset is unique in providing access to real-world data for training and testing purposes. When tested, our proposed SceneFusion algorithm, which combines a novel loss function with a deep learning-based approach, demonstrated superior reconstruction accuracy compared to current state-of-the-art techniques. This accuracy was further validated through comparisons with high-quality ground truth models and real-world measurements. Ultimately, SceneFusion is poised to play a pivotal role in driving the future development of learned multi-view 3D reconstruction methods. The prevalence of failed pixels in modern camera sensors is a known issue. Despite its importance, the effect of dead pixels on deep learning models remains unexplored. This research investigates the influence of failed pixels on two representative deep learning applications, including image classification and object detection, under simulated image degradation. A thorough examination is conducted using failure models based on both Gaussian and Poisson distributions. The results show that dead pixels have a distinct impact on different tasks and are influenced by the type of dataset used, the type of camera sensor employed, and the level of pixel failure. The research further indicates that standard convolutional neural networks can effectively adapt to image distortion caused by failed pixels and achieve improved performance during training. This adaptation, however, comes at the cost of reduced accuracy on unaltered images. The findings suggest that employing techniques like data augmentation or image correction could mitigate this performance decline and enable models trained on degraded images to generalize to real-world scenarios with improved accuracy. This study provides a foundation for future research to explore the effects of failed pixels on deep learning models and to develop strategies for mitigating performance declines. We introduce AppealNet, a novel approach to automatically adjusting the complexity-tolerance of deep learning models in response to computation constraints. Our method, based on an information theory framework, calculates the degree of model uncertainty resulting from accuracy losses due to complexity reduction. This information is used to dynamically fine-tune the model's architecture, balancing accuracy against computation cost and computational resources. AppealNet has been tested across diverse applications, including computer vision and natural language processing, with impressive computation savings of up to 60% achieved without sacrificing accuracy. Notably, our method compares favourably with established pruning and distillation techniques, requiring no supplementary training or testing phases. A long-standing debate surrounds the relationship between diversity and model performance in neural network architectures. On one hand, architectures with numerous weights and connections often yield superior results, yet these may be unnecessary for optimal performance. To resolve this question, we conducted an experiment involving a neural network with limited connections, finding that a small number of these connections, when used as probes, enables the model to effectively learn and resolve control problems without excessive parameter adjustments, significantly reducing prediction errors compared to a model with randomly selected connections, by up to 90%. The learned model components can be applied across various domains, while the probing states facilitate model interpretability. We propose that this approach can be used to improve the efficiency of neural networks for continuous control problems. By harnessing the power of fractals, our design approach offers a significant advantage over existing sparse arrays, which are often limited by their periodicity and symmetry constraints. We believe that our method will pave the way for the development of more advanced, sparse antenna arrays with enhanced capabilities. In the context of federated learning, where data is stored on personal devices and training models via wireless communication, this research investigates how to effectively train a shared model using data from multiple users. Typically, each user's training process involves sending and receiving gradients via wireless communication, which can be inefficient. To mitigate this issue, a novel approach, referred to as pFedHN, is proposed. This method utilizes a hierarchical structure, where one user acts as a coordinator and the other users report to it. Crucially, pFedHN only requires each user to transmit a single value, thereby minimizing communication costs. Notably, under certain conditions, pFedHN converges to the optimal shared model. Moreover, the performance of pFedHN is compared to other state-of-the-art methods through experiments using MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets. The results indicate that pFedHN achieves comparable accuracy while significantly reducing communication costs by a factor of 100. Additionally, the impact of pFedHN on communication costs is evaluated under different network conditions, revealing that it outperforms the baseline method by a substantial margin of up to 100 times when the channel is severely affected. Multilingual BERT's performance can be improved by fine-tuning it with a specific task in a particular language. However, the impact of fine-tuning on the model's ability to transfer knowledge to other languages remains unclear. Our study examines how fine-tuning affects both the multilingual and language-specific parts of multilingual BERT. Our analysis reveals that the model's ability to transfer knowledge to other languages is limited, especially in tasks where language and content are closely tied. This can lead to the creation of task-specific predictors that may not generalize to other tasks. As a result, we propose a method to fine-tune multilingual BERT in a language-agnostic way, which we demonstrate improves zero-shot transfer to unseen languages without compromising in-language performance. Our method can be used to make multilingual BERT more transferable without increasing training time or data. Moreover, we show that fine-tuning can be used to create models that excel in multiple tasks, but are weak in other tasks, suggesting that the extent of domain overlap between tasks affects the transferability of fine-tuned models. Our findings provide a better understanding of multilingual BERT's ability to transfer knowledge across languages and tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/salesforce/zero-shot_mBERT.

Image segmentation through variational methods is commonly applied but often 
involves solving complex non-convex problems. Specifically, the hyper-Laplacian 
image segmentation model exhibits non-convexity in its set function, making it 
challenging to determine the exact minimizer. However, by incorporating a 
perturbation to the model, we can achieve the exact minimizer using a dual 
formulation and the proximal point algorithm. Furthermore, this approach 
enables us to demonstrate the exact recovery of image segments and establish 
error bounds. Numerical experiments confirm the efficacy of this method in 
segmenting images from real-world data. Additionally, we extend our findings 
to the problem of image segmentation with multiple labels, finding that the 
exact minimizer can still be determined. However, the associated minimax problem 
becomes NP-hard due to its non-convexity, and we provide a heuristic solution 
using a proximal point algorithm with an approximation scheme. This approach 
allows us to segment images with multiple labels and demonstrates its 
applicability to real-world data through numerical experiments. Lastly, we apply 
our methods to the problem of image segmentation from single photon counting 
magnetic resonance data. By leveraging the properties of this data, we are able 
to segment the data into distinct regions and quantify the size of each region. 
This approach enables us to determine the number of regions, which can then be 
verified using a statistical test. Numerical experiments illustrate the 
effectiveness of our methods in this challenging application. All related 
code is available at https://github.com/zheng-112009/hyperlaplacian-segmentation.

magnetic resonance data is at https://github.com/zheng-112009/SPCMR-segmentation.

It is now feasible to build end-to-end neural networks that can synthesize the audio from a video based on motion and content cues. However, the performance of these networks is currently limited by the absence of large-scale datasets. To address this issue, we present a new dataset called It'sTimeToWave, which contains 16 hours of high-quality audio and video. Based on this dataset, we trained and compared different types of networks, including those that can synthesize audio and video, and found that a particular network called It$\circ$Wave outperforms current state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin, achieving a mean opinion score of 3.46. Furthermore, we found that combining two separate networks, one that can synthesize the audio and another that can synthesize the video, results in a significantly better outcome than training a single network on the entire dataset, even though it had 10 times less training data. These findings open up new possibilities for the development of more efficient and effective neural networks for video-to-audio synthesis. target positions for a robot. We then use these sequences to generate

optimized for fast performance. We tested our approach using various natural
language commands in a simulated environment and achieved a 60% success
rate with a single command. We also found that our approach can adjust to
changing user commands and can handle various types of user input commands.

Given a Hermitian matrix A in complex space and its Hermitian part A + B, we demonstrate that the convergence rate bounds of the preconditioned Arnoldi and Lanczos iterations can be applied to both A and B. 

Specifically, we derived a complex version of the Aubry-Daniel asymptotic formula and the backward error bound for the spectral Arnoldi iteration. Moreover, we generalized the convergence rate bounds for the Lanczos eigensolvers for computing eigenvalues with a prescribed accuracy. 

We also investigated the convergence rates of various preconditioned Arnoldi and Lanczos iterations for computing generalized eigenpairs. 

Numerical experiments were conducted to validate our findings and demonstrate the practical implications of the convergence rate bounds. The results indicate that the convergence rates of the preconditioned Arnoldi and Lanczos iterations are robust and unaffected by small perturbations. This has significant implications for the practical application of the preconditioned methods. 

Finally, we derived a backward error bound for the spectral Arnoldi iteration, which provides an upper bound on the norm of the perturbation term in the preconditioned Arnoldi iteration. This paper introduces MemTS, a comprehensive test suite designed to assess 
memory safety protocols in operating systems, focusing on data confidentiality, 
integrity, and availability. The test suite consists of 217 validated real-world 
scenarios, generated from 68 documented vulnerabilities in Linux and other 
publicly accessible sources. The evaluation of 14 leading safety-focused file systems, 
including seL4 and Linux kernel, reveals that only 13 of the file systems passed 
all the memory safety tests, highlighting potential security risks in the remaining 
cases. This test suite is designed as an open standard, allowing file system 
developers to accurately identify and address memory safety issues in their systems. 
The test suite's source code, documentation, and a report of the evaluation results 
are available for download at https://memts.org. The ongoing development and refinement 
of the test suite will facilitate a more secure and widely adopted file system standard.

In this study, we analyze the quasi-optimal error rates of the finite element method for nonlinear stochastic wave equations with variable coefficients and noise inputs. To derive these error estimates, we address the challenges posed by the nonlinear equations and the underlying stochastic framework, as well as the spatial and temporal discretization methods. Specifically, we employ the Milstein stochastic integral for temporal discretization, a novel approach in this context. We establish error estimates for two distinct spatial discretization methods – the discontinuous Galerkin method and the Galerkin finite element method – demonstrating that they yield optimal error rates with respect to the spatial and stochastic variables. These findings are further exemplified through numerical experiments that validate the theoretical results. Notably, our work reveals that the discretization of the Stieltjes integral can significantly impact the error estimates, necessitating further investigation. Consequently, this study contributes to the broader research area of stochastic wave equations and paves the way for future studies on other related topics. Additional theoretical and computational explorations are planned in the areas of stochastic elliptic equations, parabolic equations, and the Burgers equation. The results and insights developed in this work will serve as a valuable reference for these future investigations. To address this issue, we propose a different approach by analyzing the rate of neutrino flavor change in relation to matter density, effectively introducing a physical scale into the analysis. Using this approach, we demonstrate that, in the context of both linear and non-linear physics, the rate of decoherence due to matter is influenced by the difference in mass between the heaviest and lightest neutrinos. This difference is a key physical parameter, independent of the specific neutrino mass hierarchy. Accident prediction is a vital concern for smart city development and traffic safety. Current state-of-the-art models for accident forecasting suffer from limitations in capturing dynamic traffic conditions and spatial relationships between intersections. These models also fail to adapt to changing traffic patterns and require extensive data collection. To address these issues, we introduce the Dynamic Spatial-Temporal Attention network, which leverages deep learning to analyze traffic patterns and spatial relationships at intersections. The proposed approach outperforms previous methods by achieving a significant improvement in accident prediction accuracy, with a notable increase of 20%. Moreover, it demonstrates high efficiency in processing large datasets, even on a cloud platform with a response time of under 50ms. This allows cities to quickly identify accident-prone intersections and take proactive measures to enhance road safety. A novel optical flow estimation approach, known as SMURF, addresses the challenge of reconstructing camera motion from single image optical flow. SMURF treats the problem as an overdetermined matrix factorization task, leveraging the structure of optical flow to derive the camera motion. By utilizing a robust residual minimization technique, SMURF can effectively handle motion outside of the frame, yielding accurate and reliable results. Experimental evaluations using both synthetic and real-world datasets reveal that SMURF outperforms other methods in terms of reconstruction accuracy. Furthermore, the approach is capable of accurately estimating camera motion even in scenarios with significant motion relative to the image resolution, making it a valuable tool for applications requiring high-speed image stabilization. A real-world evaluation involving a handheld smartphone demonstrates the effectiveness of SMURF in real-world scenarios. We've found that there isn't a smooth plane model for the modular curve $\Gamma_0(N)$ when the level $N$ is a square, along the lines of the well-known Gross-Zagier conjecture. This finding, in conjunction with the Gross-Zagier, Bianchi, and Conrey conjecture, provides a constraint on the possible coefficients of $L(s,\chi)\prod_{n=1}^\infty (1-p_n^{-s})^{-a_n}$ where $p_n$ is a prime, and $a_n$ relates to the modular curve's $L$-function. Notably, our work also confirms that there's no constraint for even levels as long as $N$ is not a perfect square. This is an improvement over the Bianchi Conjecture which only holds for odd levels. Our proof leverages the self-duality of Shimura curves and the properties of Heegner points, a concept introduced by Klosowicki-Pe\~na. We've also established a similar result for Shimura curves of Abelian type, and our work is further enhanced by a broader application of the Shimura curve's self-duality principle. This allows us to show that for a specific class of Abelian varieties, there's a smooth model for their Jacobians, and their $L$-functions have a particular property: they don't vanish at any imaginary integer points. We consider a particular arrangement of points, known as a geometric (n_k) configuration, within a k-dimensional space defined by the set of points {0, 1, 2, …, n_k - 1}. This specific configuration is characterized by the requirement that any n_k - 1 points must not contain a subset of k consecutive elements. Our main result shows that for sufficiently large values of n_k and any k greater than or equal to two, such a configuration is guaranteed to exist. This finding is derived from an innovative approach that combines combinatorial arguments with probabilistic methods in number theory. Furthermore, we investigate the asymptotic behavior of n_k as it approaches infinity and demonstrate that for every k, it is possible to select a subset of points that form a geometric (n_k) configuration while minimizing the number of points used. This problem was first addressed by Erdős and Szekeres in 1965, and our research refines their initial estimate by establishing a new upper limit. Our proof leverages the idea of "random restriction" introduced by Erdős and Spencer in 1971, allowing us to derive the desired result through a process of iterative refinement. Additionally, we explore the potential for adapting this process to other related problems. This is also the first instance where the "random restriction" technique has been employed in a context where the main consideration is related to the size of the set rather than the distribution of elements within it. Our findings also extend the work of Kohaychuk and Spencer from 1986, who examined the asymptotic behavior of n_k in the case where k equals two. This research is further extended to include additional results on the generation of sequences of numbers that meet specific criteria related to the geometric (n_k) configuration. Our research delves into the Burning Number Conjecture, specifically focusing on graph classes that can be reduced to a single, universal vertex. We provide a detailed characterization of these graph classes, demonstrating that they encompass all trees, unichromatic graphs, strongly chordal graphs, and various others. Building on existing findings, we also establish that graphs characterized by being 2-degenerate, chordal, or threshold are indeed subject to the Burning Number Conjecture. Furthermore, our analysis reveals the conjecture's applicability to certain well-defined graph categories, including those dominated by specific vertex sets, while also identifying additional, smaller graph classes that satisfy the conjecture. The underlying proof strategies involve the development of an efficient, time-sensitive algorithm for determining the optimal burning time within certain graph types and the application of decomposition techniques to establish the conjecture's validity for more complex categories. The paper also outlines a range of open challenges and potential avenues for further research in this field. The associated code can be accessed via https://github.com/mfelschmandt/BurningNumberConjecture. A separate, independent proof of the conjecture's applicability to unichromatic graphs can be found in https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.01619. Ultimately, our research contributes to a deeper understanding of the Burning Number Conjecture, shedding light on the nature of the graphs that satisfy the conjecture. We introduce a novel Spatial Transformer Network designed for 3D geometric transformations. The 3D Spatial Transformer Network leverages a multi-head attention mechanism to dynamically select relevant features and capture the desired type of geometric transformations. By doing so, it inherently learns invariance to the 3D transformations and becomes a versatile tool for 3D geometric learning. We successfully integrate this module into a 3D object detection framework, achieving state-of-the-art results on the KITTI dataset. Furthermore, we demonstrate the network's robustness to different 3D transformations and its ability to learn invariance to the same transformations. The proposed module can be seamlessly integrated into any 3D deep learning architecture to acquire the desired invariance to the desired 3D transformations. The integration of machine learning (ML) into critical systems necessitates the ability to monitor these systems' safety parameters. Current ML autograding approaches, although useful, fall short when faced with complex monitoring tasks. To address this, we developed a framework that enables the creation of simple, predictive models to forecast the likelihood of safety issues arising from changes in previously evaluated data sets. By utilizing these models, we can identify potential problems in data distributions or ML models that may lead to safety breaches. For instance, we applied our framework to a critical system - autonomous driving, specifically focusing on pedestrian safety. We created predictive models to forecast the likelihood of breaching a "no collision" policy, including a more stringent "no breach" policy and a "no severe breach" policy, representing different levels of criticality. We found that significant changes in data distributions can significantly increase the likelihood of breaching the more stringent policy but may not necessarily impact the less severe one, demonstrating that traditional ML autograding methods are inadequate for monitoring safety-critical systems. Furthermore, we observed that our predictive models can identify issues that traditional autograding methods miss, highlighting the importance of using these models to monitor system safety. We also found that our approach can pinpoint specific data points or subsets that are most likely to lead to safety breaches, enabling data curators to take corrective action to prevent such breaches. Overall, our framework provides a practical method for ensuring the safety and stability of ML systems. We also believe that our framework has the potential to be applied to other critical systems and encourage further research into its use cases. The Internet of Things (IoT) has become an integral part of our daily lives, with its applications extending beyond the personal domain into public services. However, the current approach to data protection in IoT has several limitations, primarily due to its reliance on cloud-based solutions that raise concerns about data security and control. In light of these issues, we are proposing a new approach called Self-Serviced IoT (SSIoT), which aims to address the core challenges in secure IoT data management. Specifically, SSIoT seeks to enable users to fully exercise their control over personal data, eliminate the need for intermediaries in data exchange, and ensure secure data storage through advanced cryptographic techniques. Building on the principles of Self-Sovereign Identity Networks (SSINs), SSIoT presents a comprehensive framework that outlines the core features, design requirements, and potential applications of this novel framework. Our research indicates that SSIoT has the potential to overcome current limitations in IoT data management and offer a more effective solution for a wide range of IoT applications. Furthermore, we have identified and addressed the primary obstacles to implementing SSIoT, and our analysis highlights several promising areas of research, including the integration of SSIoT with other IoT frameworks, the development of SSIoT-specific protocols, and exploring the use of decentralized storage solutions for SSIoT. Ultimately, we believe that SSIoT has the potential to revolutionize the way we manage data in IoT ecosystems, and our research aims to contribute to this significant shift. The source code of SSIoT is available in public repositories on GitHub. https://github.com/andrewnguyen210/SSIoT.git. A comprehensive implementation guide for SSIoT can be found in the supplementary materials.

This research delves into the issue of discrepancies between training datasets and the task at hand. Discregencies can impede model performance on unseen tasks, particularly in translation quality and calibration. To mitigate this, our proposed method, DisCon, uses a data selection approach that leverages reference annotations to identify in-domain samples with greater discrepancies. Experimental results demonstrate that DisCon significantly enhances translation quality and calibration on multiple targets, particularly in scenarios with prominent discongruities. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that DisCon's selection strategy is effective even when working with limited reference data annotations. In contrast, traditional data selection methods, which rely on metrics such as BLEU scores, are less successful in addressing discongruities. Our findings also indicate that DisCon's reliance on reference annotations is more efficient than using metrics for selecting training data. Ultimately, our results show that DisCon's ability to pinpoint high-discongruent samples enables the development of more reliable machine translation models. processes. This package is available at https://github.com/zhengzeyu/PCRimputation.

We've developed a new method for creating adversarial representations that resist fairness constraints by combining two techniques. First, we use stacking to create a model that's aware of both data and task labels. Second, we apply dampening, a form of regularization that prevents these two sets of labels from correlating excessively. Through this process, we've found that the resulting representations become increasingly similar when subjected to the same fairness constraints, but remain distinct when facing different constraints. Notably, our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in several benchmark datasets. We've also demonstrated that our method can effectively reduce unfair bias in models while maintaining their accuracy. Overall, our findings suggest that dampening and stacking can be a powerful tool for evaluating and mitigating unfair bias in classification tasks. This method can also be extended to other forms of unfair bias, such as demographic bias, as seen in further experiments on the Bellamy et al. (2019) dataset. The research investigates how different approaches affect semantic precision, comparing scenarios where the parser is frozen during training and updated in tandem with the variational generator. We propose an innovative approach, called Max-Relevance-Min-Divergence (MRmD), 
for the development of high-performance (HP) discretization methods. 
This novel approach is grounded in the principle of minimizing divergence 
between the output probability distributions and the target distribution 
for the respective attributes. By integrating this approach with a 
multi-objective evolutionary algorithm, we create a high-performance 
discretization method, which we refer to as MRmD-EMEA. 
This method outperforms existing discretization methods for the task of 
multilabel classification on a range of benchmark datasets, 
including yeast, medical, ijcnn, covertype, and Reuters. 
Experimental results confirm that MRmD-EMEA yields high-performance 
discretization for complex datasets, enhancing the performance of various 
machine learning algorithms. Moreover, the method's adaptability is 
demonstrated through its ability to be combined with different algorithms, 
resulting in improved classification accuracy. 
This research contributes to the field of HP discretization methods, 
providing a versatile and efficient algorithm for the development of 
high-performance discretization methods. 
Additionally, the method's adaptability enables the creation of 
high-performance discretization for diverse machine learning algorithms.

The rapid digitalization of society has made digital skills education essential, yet traditional methods have struggled to scale, reaching only a small percentage of underprivileged youth. To bridge this gap, global initiatives like Code Week have been launched, offering one-week code workshops in over 200 countries. However, the effectiveness of such events has not been thoroughly assessed, particularly regarding their impact on participants. This study examines data from Code Week 2018 in Colombia and the Dominican Republic to identify socio-economic factors influencing participants' engagement and gain insights into skillful participants. Our analysis indicates that participants' socio-economic status, gender, and connection with organizers significantly impact their ability to complete code projects and demonstrate proficiency. Notably, participants' initial skill level determines their ability to improve, with more experienced individuals benefiting less from the event. These findings provide valuable information for organizers of similar digital skills formation events. Our data-driven approach also enables the development of predictive models that can help tailor initiatives to better meet the needs of underprivileged youth worldwide. This research introduces Prompt, a simple method that enables language models to control robots by executing complex manipulation tasks using text prompts alone.
Prompt builds on the established practice of visual perception in robot control by incorporating a language model to generate control commands based on visual information, eliminating the need for traditional symbolic language.
Unlike prior work, Prompt eliminates the reliance on pre-habits and instead leverages a language model to generate control commands based on visual information, eliminating the need for training or prior experience.
Prompt achieves state-of-the-art performance in both tabletop and kitchen manipulation scenarios, with the added benefit of generalizing to novel environments, objects, and scenarios, all through the use of a single model trained with minimal data. Recent studies have shown that differential privacy can be achieved in the statistical sense under specific conditions, but it remains unclear whether the resulting private algorithms are effective. This paper explores the accuracy of differentially private predictions in various private learning settings, revealing that simple post-processing techniques can yield high-performing methods. Contrary to expectations, empirical results indicate that differential privacy parameterized Lasso methods excel when compared to more straightforward methods like the clipped Gaussian mechanism. Notably, the accuracy of these methods surpasses previously established private methods, such as those based on the Gaussian mechanism and adaptive clipping with rejection. These findings hold across multiple private learning settings, including regression, classification, and clustering, and suggest that post-processing techniques can be effectively applied to existing private methods. Consequently, the development and optimization of private learning methods may now focus on achieving differential privacy through alternative approaches rather than directly optimizing differential privacy guarantees. This research has significant implications for the field of private machine learning, as it provides a potential solution to the accuracy vs. utility trade-offs. A key challenge in neural architecture analysis is measuring pairwise distances.  However, existing metrics often rely on time-consuming and redundant calculations of architecture representations.  To address this issue, we introduce a novel strategy for optimizing architecture comparisons by exploiting connections between set operations and Markov algebras. Previous approaches to detecting concurrency issues in Go programs have significant limitations as they rely heavily on program locations, resulting in numerous false positives and making it difficult to identify the root cause of bugs. To overcome this, we developed a novel approach, called GO-SLICER, which leverages dynamic race checking and source-level analysis simultaneously. Specifically, GO-SLICer employs a dynamic race detector for Go programs and, at the same time, uses a source-level incremental inter-procedural cutter to identify true concurrency bugs. This latter component is a novel technique, which cuts program call chains based on source-level control, procedural relationships, and program dynamics. By integrating these two analyses, GO-SLICER is able to effectively reduce false positives and provide accurate results. In evaluating GO-SLICER on 12 real-world Go applications, we found that it successfully identified 52 concurrency issues, including 31 unique bugs, and among them, 29 were confirmed as real bugs. Furthermore, 30 out of 42 of its reported issues were reproducible and 28 out of 42 were considered serious security threats. Additionally, GO-SLICER outperformed 7 other approaches in terms of both effectiveness and efficiency by a significant margin. To further validate its effectiveness, we also conducted a human study involving 10 participants and found that GO-SLICER was significantly more efficient in identifying concurrency issues than other approaches. To our knowledge, this is the first source-level inter-procedural cutter for concurrent programs, and we plan to publicly release its source code soon. The ability of natural language processing models to apply learned patterns from training data to real-world utterances is crucial for practical deployment. We investigate how training data is affected by three key elements: (1) the presence of human observers who provide feedback to the model, (2) the use of human-annotated examples, and (3) the model's ability to improve itself. A comprehensive experiment reveals that model performance is significantly enhanced by human oversight and the incorporation of manually-verified examples, surpassing that of human-annotated data alone. Furthermore, our results indicate that self-improving models benefit from the presence of human observers but do not exhibit improved performance without additional human-verified training examples. Notably, our findings suggest that model self-improvement alone may not fully utilize human oversight, and the combination of human-verified examples and model self-improvement yields superior results. Ultimately, our study demonstrates that an approach combining human observers, example-driven training, and model self-improvement enables natural language processing models to achieve superior generalizability. This research contributes to the development of more capable NLP models, and we believe that our findings have significant implications for the deployment of such models in real-world applications. We propose a novel approach to analyzing call graphs that change over time, 
building upon call graph matching techniques. This method uses Call Graph 
Evolution Rules and Call Graph Evolution Subgraphs to track the development 
of call relationships within a program. We introduce a way to represent these 
evolving call graphs, allowing us to identify specific patterns based on these 
patterns and subpatterns. We then develop a technique to identify the most 
relevant patterns by measuring their influence on the call graph's evolution. 
Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through an evaluation 
on a dataset of 700 Java projects. This involved applying our technique to 1, 
500 issue-resolution events, enabling us to pinpoint the most relevant patterns 
and use them to predict whether an issue was resolved or not. We also found 
that our approach outperformed a baseline method. While our approach is effective 
for small to medium-sized projects, we acknowledge that it can be improved 
for larger projects. We also recognize that our approach can be enhanced with 
further research. This paper will be a 12-page submission, and some figures, 
tables, and additional details are provided in an accompanying 4-page supplement.

This paper introduces an innovative system for automating legal reasoning, 
built around a legal expert system that draws information from a lawyer 
through an interactive questioning method. The process commences when the 
programmer formulates an inquiry based on a specific legal issue and then 
conducts an interview with a lawyer who responds with relevant information 
relevant to the issue at hand. The program then utilizes this information 
to generate a legal argument in a format that mimics a lawyer's written 
brief. The primary contribution of this research lies in the development 
of a novel approach to automating legal reasoning, referred to as Legal 
Questioning. The proposed method involves formulating an inquiry, gathering 
 relevant information from a human expert, and leveraging this data to 
craft a well-informed legal argument. The implementation of this method 
is demonstrated through the design of a system called Legal Argument 
Creation, which is showcased in the context of an application involving 
US tax law. The paper also reports on the system's performance in a 
benchmark test and offers further directions for the continued research

In the context of convex bodies, Kloeckner's (2016) inequality is adapted to establish a logarithmically submodular volume function for specified subsets K. Additionally, we examine under what conditions the proposed submodular volume function could be extended to a continuous setting. Lastly, we present empirical results demonstrating the sharpness of the established logarithmically submodular inequalities. This research is a key outcome of the second author's Ph.D. work. We categorize representations of Bol algebras that are two-dimensional, 
proving there are only six non-trivial examples. This work extends and 
includes more comprehensive understanding of the ones previously known. 
Furthermore, our analysis reveals Bol algebras can be fully defined through 
their automorphisms, specifically those from the Bol-Boltenkov family and 
the singular Bol-Jacobi algebra, where the latter is shown to be 
non-representable through a straightforward method. Similarly, we show that 
the Bol-Almeida-Morimoto algebra cannot be represented in the same manner. 
Lastly, we explore and describe the primary Lie algebras that are the 
underlying base of the Bol algebras we examined.

Gumbel-softmax algorithms have been widely adopted in machine learning literature but a lack of theoretical understanding exists in regards to their convergence rate. This research aims to bridge the gap by examining the convergence rate of Gumbel-sigmoid for Dirichlet allocation under specific conditions. First, we consider a simplified version of the Dirichel allocation with only two free parameters. By using Stein's method and analyzing the convergence rate, we establish that it converges at a $\mathcal{O}(1/n)$ rate under certain regular conditions. Next, we prove that Dirichlet allocation converges at a $\mathcal{O}(1/n^{1/2})$ rate under a more general setting that relaxes the previous assumptions. This research provides a theoretical explanation for why Gumbel-sigmoid outperforms its softmax counterpart in various applications. Furthermore, we establish a theoretical connection between Gumbel-sigmoid and the gradient descent method when using Laplace-Metropolis Hastings sampling, which explains its effectiveness in optimization tasks. The features from these localized encoders are combined and decoded by a main decoder to produce a more accurate depth map. Software systems often include conditional code and configuration settings that remain unchanged even after installation, consuming resources and complicating maintenance. These unutilized options can lead to security vulnerabilities if malicious users can manipulate them, which they might when the options' values are hard-coded and shared across user accounts. Our approach, Value Sharing Normalization, identifies and rectifies such value sharing instances in Java software, thereby reducing their susceptibility to attacks and freeing up resources such as memory. For instance, a specific instance of value sharing that we addressed in the Apache Tomcat and Apache HttpComponents Client projects, affecting over 80% of their user base, was converted to use distinct values for each application context, resulting in a 5% reduction in memory usage in the Apache Tomcat project. Our evaluation shows that Value Sharing Normalization is feasible, effective, and does not negatively impact the performance of software systems. Our methodology for assessing AI video compression across multiple datasets is now available, and we plan to release our framework as open-source software. This framework includes the BPFV codec, evaluation scripts, and datasets, thereby enabling the research and development of future high-performance AI video compression systems. We find that the interaction between localized magnetic moments and itinerant Ru-$d$ states is critical in explaining the material's ground state, where the Ru-$d$ states exhibit a strong magnetic moment, resulting in an anisotropic magnetic interaction that supports multiple magnetic phases, including a spin glass state. Our results are in agreement with experimental findings, providing a unified explanation for the material's properties and identifying potential areas for further investigation. Notably, Mn$_2$RuGa offers an exceptional model system for exploring the interplay between strong Ru-$d$ states and strong spin-orbit coupling, where the latter is significantly enhanced by the presence of Ga. Our study highlights the potential of Mn$_2$RuGa to serve as a paradigm for understanding the interplay between these two dominant effects in condensed matter systems. Additionally, Mn$_2$RuGa presents an intriguing platform for the discovery of novel magnetic phases, magnetoelectric effects, and topological properties, offering a unique opportunity to explore the interplay of multiple quantum phenomena. Finally, we propose that the Mn$_2$RuGa system could be utilized to study the effects of strong spin-orbit coupling in Weyl, Weyl-Dirac, and topological semimetallic phases, and to explore the interplay of topological properties and quantum phenomena such as superconductivity and topological superconductivity. We introduce an approach to enhancing the manipulation of garments through
interacting with a robot arm simulator. Our method enhances manually-created
techniques by adjusting key parameters to make them more efficient and adaptable
to various garments. To quantify the performance of manipulation policies, we assess
their effectiveness in minimizing manipulation attempts and preserving garment
integrity. Our results show that the proposed policy outperforms existing methods,
yielding a 2.3-fold reduction in manipulation attempts and a 25% decrease in garment
damage when manipulating a cotton t-shirt. Additionally, the versatility of our
approach enables its application to diverse garments without requiring retraining,
allowing for seamless transfer and generalization. To facilitate the reproduction
of our results, we provide access to the trained agents and video demonstrations
online. We also present a policy tailored for the Dexterity Challenge and share a
policy file for use in the challenge. To support further research, we will release
our simulator, training code, and other resources after publication. This study
paves the way for future research in policy-based manipulation and addresses the
need for more efficient and garment-friendly manipulation techniques. To this
end, we encourage the community to participate in the challenge by developing
competing policies. Our research materials can be found in the supplementary
materials.

The Bhojpuri, Magahi, and Maithili languages are part of the Hindi family and widely spoken in Bihar and Jharkhand, India. Despite their limited resources, these languages have a significant number of native speakers - over 70 million individuals. In this research, we present innovative approaches to developing language technology for these under-resourced languages. We introduce and share 10,000 Maithili sentences along with their English translations, collected from a multiple-choice quiz context. Furthermore, we compare the performance of Maithili language models on two tasks: sentence similarity and word similarity. Additionally, we release a Maithili translation dataset based on multiple-choice quiz responses and analyze its quality, achieving 71% accuracy in verification. We also introduce Bhojpuri and Magahi language models, applying multiple training techniques to improve their performance. Finally, we conduct cross-lingual transfer experiments, demonstrating that pre-training is beneficial for these languages. The Bhojpuri data set and language models are released at https://github.com/IIITMx/Maithili-Translation-Data and https://huggingface.co/IIITMx/Magahi, respectively. Notably, our approach yields more accurate results and significantly reduces errors associated with approximate fermion-to-boson transformations. We've also introduced a dynamic selection process that ensures high-quality approximations are consistently applied. Furthermore, our method can be adapted to accommodate a wide range of approximate contraction schemes with varying levels of accuracy, making it an ideal framework for approximate fermion-to-boson transformations.
