The connection between a skilled user's actions and an automated system they're interacting with can be likened to the concept of control, where the user's actions are the input that drives the system. This concept is explored in the context of Human-Computer Interaction (HCI), where various aspects, such as devices and interfaces, are analyzed using Optimal Feedback Control (OFC) theory. A key principle of OFC is that optimal performance is achieved when systems learn and adapt under specific conditions, an idea that is often misunderstood in HCI applications. This paper aims to clarify these misconceptions, provide an overview of OFC, and demonstrate its relevance and implications through various examples in HCI settings. Furthermore, it presents a unified framework for understanding different approaches to human-machine interaction, models human behavior in various scenarios, and highlights the potential of OFC for improving our understanding of HCI. Ultimately, it argues that OFC offers a valuable framework for designing and evaluating effective HCI systems. This paper is a revised and expanded version of the author's earlier work, "Optimal Feedback Control for Human-Machine Interaction: A Unifying Theory", published in IEEE Control Systems Society. This paper investigates how a remote user with state information and a wireless sensor system interact with a potential eavesdropper in a multi-party setting under a physical layer security framework. Unfortunately, there's a lack of standardized guidelines for reporting and sharing robot incident data, and there's limited access to historical robot accident data. To address this issue, we're proposing the Open Robot Investigation Database (ORID) as an open standard for reporting and sharing robot incident data. This proposed standard comprises a data structure and a format for reporting and sharing robot incident data. We demonstrate the practical application of ORID through a case study of a robot falling over and make our proposal openly accessible online. This initiative is also supported by a community-based forum to discuss and refine the standard. By implementing this open standard, we can create a safer robot system by learning from past robot incidents. In a rapidly evolving cyber threat landscape, sophisticated attacks can conceal their presence by not producing noticeable, patterned behavior, such as a sudden increase in traffic immediately after a malware deployment. However, a typical attack pattern typically involves a gradual build-up before a peak, followed by a decline. Given this challenge, our research introduces a novel approach that combines a statistical model of normal network traffic with a Bayesian change-point detection model. This approach enables real-time network traffic analysis, identifying potential threats not detected by conventional methods, including signature-based and anomaly detection tools. Through our evaluation, we found that this method successfully identifies the underlying cause of a cyber attack, including the type of attack and machine involved, in scenarios with limited network data. Moreover, our approach provides clear, interpretable results, in stark contrast to deep learning-based methods that can produce unclear, black-box results. To support this research, we have made our evaluation dataset and code publicly accessible for further study and use. Additionally, we have released a new, simplified dataset specifically designed to simulate cyber attack scenarios. Our work is expected to facilitate the development of advanced, automated threat detection systems that can respond proactively to emerging cyber threats in real-time. ensuring continuous refinement of the interpretation.

This study introduces a groundbreaking open set detection framework that can adapt to new classes without retraining. It leverages the idea that samples from unknown classes exhibit distinct features from seen classes. A novel optimization problem is formulated to generate artificial samples with varying densities for different classes, thus enriching the training set. These pseudo-unseen samples are then used to train a classifier, yielding superior open set detection performance across various domains. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both image and speech recognition tasks with significant margins in accuracy. In real-world applications, time series data often exhibits correlations that change over time and features that require modeling through non-linear and non-autoregressive representations. Piecewise stationary models offer an effective solution by assuming the time series data is composed of segments with stationary characteristics and using a hidden process to identify these segments. This approach, however, raises a key issue - how to determine the optimal segment segmentation. This problem is addressed through a proposed Bayesian methodology that integrates autoregressive models with non-parametric segment prior distributions. Utilizing variational approximation techniques, specifically a gradient-based algorithm, yields a computationally efficient method for inferring model parameters. Experimental results demonstrate the proposed framework's ability to capture both segment correlations and segment patterns in synthetic and real-world datasets. This approach is further extended to account for missing data and is evaluated using simulation studies and case studies on two datasets with missing values. Ultimately, the proposed Bayesian non-parametric model offers a versatile solution for analyzing time series data with missing values. The model's implementation is available in the R package RPieceWise. This package can be downloaded from the CRAN repository. This research introduces a novel dataset, AMSSC, comprising a series of social engineering trials designed to support the development of advanced social engineering computer systems. The dataset comprises over 1,700 recorded conversations between simulated attackers and victims, alongside expert-annotated transcripts detailing key interactions, including questions, statements with question-like intent, and relevant information extracted from these interactions. By developing sophisticated algorithms to identify and dissect these interactions, this study lays the groundwork for enhanced systems capable of generating responses in real-time, facilitating the development of advanced social engineering tools. Experimental findings demonstrate that improved detection and analysis of these interactions yield significantly better outcomes in response generation, outperforming a leading NLP model by 5.2 and 4.3 percent respectively in response quality and relevance assessments. This research presents a novel neural network architecture for estimating dense
depth maps from stereo images, which is trained end-to-end without the need for
supervised learning. Our architecture, called cost constructor, generates an
estimated cost volume by analyzing an input stereo image pair. This process
incorporates a residual learning module that takes into account occlusions by
identifying disparities in both the target and background areas. Our model is
trained on the KITTI dataset and yields competitive results in both
disparity estimation and depth estimation, while also being trainable without
supervision. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our cost constructor can be used
to train a depth estimator in a self-supervised manner. Notably, our approach
performs well even when the right image of the stereo pair is unavailable. This
research showcases that a cost constructor can effectively generate a cost volume
for depth estimation and that it can be trained efficiently using self-supervision.
